paras: The lynching of Tom Forsythe took place at Carthage, Panola County, Texas, on the night of February 28-29, 1888, when about 400 men took the sheriff's son from jail and hanged him. Forsythe had been arrested days earlier and was reported to have confessed to the murder and robbery of County Treasurer D. C. Hill. The case drew notice because the lynchers acted unmasked and laid the body in the victim's blood, and because Governor Ross rebuked them.

On February 10, Treasurer Hill was found dead in his Carthage office with his head nearly severed and about $6,000 missing; the sheriff, the accused man's father, led the posse that followed. Eugene Wyley was arrested on suspicion, and suspicion also fell on a Black barber, Tippett, near whose yard young Forsythe claimed to have found stolen silver.

Howell Parker, a U.S. deputy marshal from Longview, came to suspect Forsythe, about 21 or 22, who had acted as his father's deputy. Parker let him believe the barber was the target, watched him lose money gambling, and shadowed him to silver buried in a thicket. According to the Longview correspondent, his arrest was put off 'on account of this young man's social standing' until the evidence was overwhelming.

Arrested about noon on February 27, Forsythe at first tried to blame Tippett, then called the barber innocent. In the courthouse the next day, with the jail said to be under armed guard, he confessed to an excited crowd that he had struck Hill with an axe and cut his throat while the court was adjourned for dinner.

About 10 o'clock that night a large body of men took him from the jail by force; he offered no resistance and 'begged only to be spared death by fire.' With his arms pinioned and his mother and sister praying nearby, he climbed a ladder against the tree, took a drink of water from one of Hill's sons, who had adjusted the rope, and jumped at the word, breaking his neck. The Longview account stressed that no masks were used and moonlight revealed 'the familiar features of about 400 of Panola county's best citizens.'

Once he was cut down, the lynchers laid the body in the blood stains in the treasurer's office where Hill had died. Friends then prepared the body for burial; business houses closed for the funeral, and the body was taken to Beckville for interment.

On March 5 Governor Ross wrote Judge J. H. Long of Carthage that the reward had been 'justly earned' and would be paid. He nonetheless called the lynching 'an unwise proceeding; made without sufficient cause' and 'anarchy, pure and simple.' No report of an inquest, arrests or indictments of the lynchers appears in the coverage. One Longview report added that Forsyth had planted money in the yard of the barber, Carter Tibbett, and that Tibbett 'came near' being lynched.

Texas papers carried long specials, while Northern papers from Connecticut to Dakota ran one-line briefs, two of which placed Carthage in Missouri. The Carthage wire, reprinted in Ohio and Kentucky, stressed that Forsythe asked to execute himself, under heads such as 'A Texas Criminal Assists a Band of Lynchers in His Own Execution.'

The Fort Worth Gazette's correspondent described the lynchers as neighbors 'who with sorrowful faces meted out justice,' and its editorial page judged that Forsythe 'met his just deserts' and 'it is difficult to blame the people,' while calling the act 'anarchy.'

The San Marcos Free Press, reprinting the Huntsville Item's account under 'Anarchy in Texas,' praised the governor's protest but said he had scarcely mentioned the killing of seven Black people at Spanish Camp in Wharton County. The San Antonio Light went further, arguing that the murder of seven 'colored citizens' deserved as strong a denunciation as 'the lynching of one white murdered [murderer] whose cold blooded crime was confessed.'

Accounts differ on the hour: February 29 specials put the hanging at 10 p.m. the night before, the Carthage wire said 'an early hour yesterday morning,' and a Fort Worth editorial said 'in daytime.' The Wheeling Intelligencer's report of '400 masked men' conflicts with the Texas specials, which said no masks were used.

accounts.gist: About 400 unmasked local men took Forsythe from jail about 10 p.m., hanged him in the court yard by moonlight with his mother and sister praying nearby, then laid his body in Hill's blood; friends buried him.

accounts.label: Carthage/St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: At an early hour the morning after his confession, 400 men forced the jail, hanged him from a tree in the jail yard after he asked to execute himself, and laid the body on the blood spots in the treasurer's office.

accounts.label: Governor Ross
accounts.gist: Forsythe was 'certainly guilty', but the people of Panola county had courts at hand and acted without sufficient cause; the reward would still be paid.

framing.detail: The Fort Worth daily gazette called the lynching 'anarchy' and 'a grave wrong' yet said Forsythe 'met his just deserts' and 'it is difficult to blame the people'; its news columns said the neighbors 'meted out justice'.
The Waco daily examiner ran Ross's letter under 'A Ringing Denunciation'; the San Marcos Free Press headed its piece 'Anarchy in Texas' and called the particulars 'revolting'.

The San Antonio daily light called the lynching lawless and barbarous but argued the murder of seven Black citizens in Wharton county deserved louder denunciation than 'the lynching of a confessed murderer'.

The Austin weekly statesman headlined 'Lynch Law' and called Forsythe 'The Villain' who 'Begged Piteously'; the Courier-Journal's wire head read 'A Texas Criminal Assists a Band of Lynchers in His Own Execution'.
Northern papers ran one-line briefs in news digests, some misplacing Carthage in Missouri.
